Survival less than 3 months

Comorbidities heart, renal, liver disease

QOL scale > 6 on 1-10

Lack of control of severe pain

Severe lameness

d_sv_content.name: Electrochemotherapy for Bone Cancer
d_sv_content.description:
Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).


Curr Oncol. 2022 Mar 4;29(3):1672-1682. doi: 10.3390/curroncol29030139.

Electrochemotherapy Is Effective in the Treatment of Bone Metastases

Laura Campanacci 1, Luca Cevolani 1, Francesca De Terlizzi 2, Laura Saenz 3, Nikolin Alì 1, Giuseppe Bianchi 1, Davide Maria Donati 1


Abstract

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the use of ECT in patients with metastatic bone disease, demonstrating that it does not damage the mineral structure of the bone and its regenerative capacity, and that is feasible and efficient for the treatment of bone metastases. Since 2009, 88 patients with bone metastasis have received ECT at the Rizzoli Institute. 2014 saw the start of a registry of patients with bone metastases treated with ECT, whose data are recorded in a shared database. We share the Rizzoli Institute experience of 38 patients treated with ECT for a bone metastasis, excluding patients not included in the registry (before 2014) and those treated with bone fixation. Mean follow-up was 2 months (1-52). Response to treatment using RECIST criteria was 29% objective responses, 59% stable disease, and 16% progressive disease. Using PERCIST, the response was 36% OR, 14% SD, and 50% PD with no significant differences between the two criteria. A significant decrease in pain and better quality of life was observed at follow up.


Clinical protocol: Patient will be anesthetized and the lytic area of bone to be treated identified. Using a Jamshidi bone needle, a core will be created allowing placement of the linear bone electrode into the lesion. Once in place, targeted electrochemotherapy will be applied into the lytic lesion. Bleomycin will be injected IV and after 8 minutes the pulse will be sent into the bone lesion allowing a transient opening of the cell membrane. 2- 3 treatments will be completed and the area wrapped upon recovery.


Follow up imaging in 4 and 8 weeks with radiographs.
